name: Hematite
physical: Traditionally associated with circulation of energy
Kept nearby for stamina and vitality
Linked by crystal healers to feeling anchored in the body
summary: Hematite is a heavy, mirror-bright iron oxide used as the classic grounding stone for focus, courage and steady energy, with blood-red streak and magnetic lore.
intro: Hematite is a silvery-grey stone with a heavy, cold feel and a metallic shine that looks like polished gunmetal. In nature it can be steel-grey crystals, rosettes called iron roses, shining botryoidal masses known as kidney ore, or earthy red rock. Even the metallic grey kind leaves a red-brown streak when scratched on porcelain, which is how it earned its name. Most hematite jewelry and tumbled stones are polished from dense massive pieces, and many shop items are man-made hematine with magnetic properties. Crystal lovers cherish hematite for its grounding, mirror-like presence.
history: The name comes from the Greek haima, blood, because powdered hematite stains water red. Hematite has been used for tens of thousands of years as red ochre pigment in cave paintings and burial ceremonies. Egyptians and Romans carved it into seals and amulets, and it is the main iron ore, powering the world's steel industry. Mirrors made of polished hematite have been found in ancient cultures. In the Victorian era, hematite jewelry became popular as mourning wear. Its modern role in crystal healing is as a grounding stone for the root chakra.
meaning: Crystal healers call hematite the grounding stone. It is linked to the root and earth star chakras and used to bring scattered thoughts back down to earth. Practitioners say it provides focus, courage and a sense of steady strength, which is why it is popular with people who work in high-stress environments. Its mirror finish is read as a symbol of reflection, bouncing back negative energy and encouraging honest self-assessment. Emotionally it is used for easing overwhelm, nervousness and the feeling of floating. Traditionally it is associated with balanced energy circulation and stamina. Many carry it after meditation, to return fully to the room.
howToUse: Carry a hematite tumble in your pocket on days when focus is difficult or you feel spacey. Hold one after meditation to settle back into the body. Wear a hematite bracelet or ring for steady grounding. Place a piece at the feet while lying down for a body-based grounding exercise. Add hematite to a grid with smoky quartz and black tourmaline for a strong grounding layout. Keep a stone on the desk as a calm anchor.
care: Hematite is fairly hard but brittle, and it can rust if left wet for long periods. A quick rinse is fine, but dry thoroughly. Avoid saltwater and harsh chemicals, and keep from long soaking. Cleanse with sound, breath, smoke, moonlight or sun, and set on a selenite plate if you like. Store separately, because polished surfaces scratch more easily than quartz, and avoid hard drops since it can chip.
identify: Natural hematite is heavy, with a red-brown streak on unglazed porcelain. Magnetic hematite sold in shops is usually hematine, a man-made material made of iron oxide and binders, and it often sticks strongly to a magnet. Real hematite is only weakly magnetic or not at all. Fakes may be glass or painted stone. If a streak test gives a red-brown line, it is likely genuine hematite. Hematite is rarely dyed, but it is often polished and sometimes coated.

faq.a: In crystal tradition hematite is used for grounding, focus and steady courage. People carry it in a pocket, wear it as jewelry, or hold it after meditation to return to the body and the present moment.
Most strongly magnetic hematite in shops is hematine, a man-made product. Natural hematite is only weakly magnetic. A red-brown streak on porcelain is the classic way to confirm real hematite.
A brief rinse is fine, but dry it thoroughly, since hematite is an iron oxide and can show rust stains if left wet or in salt water. Cleansing with sound, smoke or moonlight is a safer routine.
